section.title: Principal work begins by defining the problem
section.deck: Ilya Grigorik describes senior technical agency, versatility across execution styles, and the resilience of a broad skill portfolio.

blocks.question: What distinguishes principal and distinguished engineering?
answer: Grigorik resists a fixed checklist for principal engineers. At that level, defining useful work is part of the job. He expects someone entering an unfamiliar organization to understand its landscape, locate problems, form relationships with directors and other partners, and determine where their skills can help. His seven-day reconnaissance analogy emphasizes agency rather than a literal universal deadline.

Distinguished work adds evidence of dynamic range. Technically, someone must be able to reconstruct constraints from low-level implementation while also understanding business requirements and translating them into useful changes. Equally important is choosing an execution style that matches the problem.

At a frontier, rapid experiments reveal what is unknown: act, observe, adjust, and repeat. A platform API with consequences for a partner ecosystem years later needs slower, more deliberate analysis. Even there, divergent exploration must converge into an actionable recommendation. He compares distinguished expectations to a VP’s responsibility for difficult, irregular problems that lower layers could not resolve.

His broader career philosophy is to become the only person able to combine a useful portfolio of skills, rather than always compete to be the best at one specialty. He respects specialists, but thinks broad combinations can be more resilient when a field, company, or market changes.

blocks.question: Does “be the only” mean combining multiple skills to handle ambiguous situations?
answer: Yes. He illustrates it with his own ability to combine modest design, sales, support, hosting, security, and engineering skills to create something useful without assembling a large team. When a true specialist joins, he can hand over that component and redirect his attention.

Learning enough of another domain to understand its language can make cross-functional work possible. He recalls reading many marketing books to converse with marketing colleagues, while writing experience helped with PR. His estimates about acquiring a high fraction of competence quickly express a heuristic rather than a measured universal learning curve.

The senior person need not be the most knowledgeable. Grigorik’s role can be to understand platform fundamentals and business needs, identify the people who know the implementation details, and help them navigate the decision. Pattern recognition, knowing where to find answers, and facilitating the right expertise are different from memorizing every API.

Management experience provides another usable skill: an IC can temporarily coach or give feedback with an understanding of managers’ concerns. The portfolio matters because it lets someone change how they contribute as the problem changes.

followups.question: Should ICs try management, and can they return?
answer: He encourages a team-lead role as a way to learn, and management itself if it suits the person. He rejects treating the transition as one-way or viewing a return to IC work as a demotion. Managers sometimes remember being happiest before taking the next role, even while valuing what management taught them. Organizations should let people carry those skills across roles without penalty.
